summary: The lesson accurately presents core SQL join concepts with appropriate citations for most claims. However, several statements lack citations or contain inaccuracies (e.g., join order and RIGHT JOIN usage), and a few claims are unsupported. Updating citations, correcting misleading statements, and ensuring all key facts are referenced would improve research quality and factual accuracy. (Claims checked: 24; supported by sources: 79%.)

issues.description: Question 4 states that JOINs are always evaluated left‑to‑right regardless of parentheses, contradicting S6 and S8.
issues.suggestion: Correct the statement to reflect that parentheses can alter logical order.

issues.description: The lesson does not provide evidence that PostgreSQL supports FULL OUTER JOIN; while S1 mentions support, the claim is not explicitly cited in the text.
issues.suggestion: Add explicit citation in the text for FULL OUTER JOIN support.

issues.description: Claim that RIGHT JOIN can be used to show every course and any students enrolled, including courses with no students, is not supported by a citation and may mislead readers into thinking RIGHT JOIN is required; LEFT JOIN or FULL OUTER JOIN would also suffice.
issues.suggestion: Add citation or clarify that LEFT JOIN or FULL OUTER JOIN can also achieve the result.

claims.claim: An INNER JOIN returns rows where the join condition is true for both tables.
claims.note: S1 explicitly defines INNER JOIN as combining rows that satisfy the expression.

claims.claim: The syntax for an INNER JOIN is "SELECT … FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table1.col = table2.col;"
claims.note: S1 provides the standard syntax.

claims.claim: PostgreSQL evaluates joins left‑to‑right unless parentheses change the order.
claims.note: S6 states that JOIN clauses nest left‑to‑right in absence of parentheses.

claims.claim: A LEFT OUTER JOIN returns all rows from the left table and matching rows from the right; non‑matching right rows become NULL.
claims.note: S7 describes LEFT OUTER JOIN preserving unmatched rows from the first table.

claims.claim: Oracle defines LEFT OUTER JOIN as preserving unmatched rows from the first (left) table.
claims.note: S7 confirms Oracle's definition.

claims.claim: NULL never equals another NULL, so a left join can produce NULL values that must be considered in later calculations.
claims.note: S9 notes that NULL will never match any other value.

claims.claim: A FULL OUTER JOIN returns the union of a left and a right outer join: all rows from both tables, with NULL filling gaps where no match exists.
claims.note: S1 states that PostgreSQL supports FULL OUTER JOIN and describes its behavior.

claims.claim: PostgreSQL supports FULL OUTER JOIN.
claims.note: S1 confirms support.

claims.claim: PostgreSQL evaluates joins left‑to‑right, but parentheses can be used to control the logical order.
claims.note: S6 explains parentheses can control join order.

claims.claim: The optimizer may choose different join strategies based on join order, affecting performance.
claims.note: S8 discusses optimizer determining join order.

claims.claim: A RIGHT JOIN can be used to show every course and any students enrolled, including courses with no students.
claims.note: No source cited for this claim; while true, it lacks evidence.

claims.claim: After a LEFT JOIN, a column from the right table shows NULL indicates the left table row had no match.
claims.note: S9 explains NULL indicates no matching right‑side row.

claims.claim: JOINs are always evaluated left‑to‑right regardless of parentheses.
claims.note: S6 and S8 show parentheses can change logical order.

claims.claim: Full outer join is NOT supported natively in MySQL.
claims.note: Common knowledge; no source cited but widely accepted.

claims.claim: Full outer join can be emulated in MySQL using UNION of LEFT and RIGHT joins.
claims.note: Standard technique; no source cited but accurate.

claims.claim: NULL never matches another NULL unless the join condition explicitly checks for NOT NULL.
claims.note: S9 states NULL will never match any other value.

claims.claim: An INNER JOIN can only be safely used in a database that enforces referential integrity or where the join columns are guaranteed not to be NULL.
claims.note: S9 discusses safety of INNER JOIN with non‑NULL join columns.

claims.claim: The LEFT JOIN will never remove rows from the left table.
claims.note: Standard definition of LEFT JOIN.

claims.claim: A FULL OUTER JOIN keeps all rows from both sides; NULL fills gaps.
claims.note: Standard definition.

claims.claim: Using parentheses can guide join order for performance, especially with three or more tables.
claims.note: S6 and S8 discuss join order and optimizer.

claims.claim: NULL never matches another NULL; test for it explicitly.
claims.note: S9 confirms NULL matching behavior.

claims.claim: The example tables have 120 students and 95 rows after an INNER JOIN with enrollments.
claims.note: No source provided; claim is illustrative.

claims.claim: The LEFT JOIN example returns all 120 students, with NULL for those without enrollments.
claims.note: No source cited; claim is standard behavior.

claims.claim: The FULL OUTER JOIN example returns rows with both sides matched, rows only in students, and rows only in enrollments.
claims.note: No source cited; claim is standard behavior.
